analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off southwestern Florida and buys back existing leases.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Florida's two senators with one cosponsor, never left the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from selling, exploring, or developing any new oil and gas leases on the Outer Continental Shelf off Florida south of 26 degrees north latitude — roughly the waters from around Tampa Bay down past the Keys and along the state's Gulf side. For any leases already sold in that zone, the federal government would have bought them back from the leaseholders, with Congress declaring that buyback its own responsibility and authorizing whatever money it took. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal residents, beach tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing interests, who are exposed to the risk of oil spills and drilling-related industrialization if leases are sold and developed in the waters off the state's southwest coast.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities and beach tourism

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the Interior Secretary from any preleasing or leasing activity, including calls for information, tract selection, notices of sale, receipt of bids, and lease awards, on all submerged federal lands south of 26 degrees north latitude and east of 86 degrees west longitude off Florida [S3].
It also barred approval of any exploration plans or development and production plans in that same zone, closing off the paths by which already-sold leases could move toward drilling [S3].

It directed the Secretary of the Interior to issue guidelines for the United States to buy back any existing oil and gas leases in the zone, declaring the buyback the federal government's sole responsibility [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the buyback of existing leases at whatever price the courts and negotiations set, and the oil and gas industry, which would lose access to a large area of potentially productive federal waters and to the leases it already held there.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers funding lease buybacks, and oil companies

drawbacks.text: The bill put the full cost of buying back existing leases on the federal government, authorizing 'such sums as may be necessary' — an open-ended appropriation paid by taxpayers to compensate leaseholders [S3].

By barring both new leasing and development of existing leases in the zone, it would remove a source of domestic oil and gas production, which in 1990 meant greater reliance on imported petroleum, a concern the Gulf War-era Congress took seriously.

The prohibition covered only waters south of 26 degrees north latitude and east of 86 degrees west longitude, leaving other portions of the eastern Gulf of Mexico open to leasing, so protection stopped at a mapped line rather than at the edge of spill risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida's coast, the upside was large and durable: a statutory ban on drilling in the waters that drive the state's beach tourism and fishing economy, plus a path to extinguish existing leases. The main cost was honest but bounded — compensating leaseholders out of federal funds — and the bill itself acknowledged that obligation by writing the buyback into its text. The larger loss was that none of it happened.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Connie Mack introduced the bill on June 28, 1990, for himself and Sen. Bob Graham, Florida's two senators from opposite parties [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further entry of any kind after the referral; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].
The bill's one cosponsor was a Senate Democrat, recorded on the cosponsorship page [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests with existing leases or ambitions in the eastern Gulf of Mexico off Florida, since the area stayed open and no leases had to be bought back. Floridians who wanted the waters protected gained nothing from the bill's death, though the region remained undrilled for other reasons during this period.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests holding Gulf leases

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban leasing and development off southwestern Florida and to buy back existing leases with federal funds.

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.what_they_did: Joined Mack in introducing the bill; the cosponsorship record shows him as the bill's one Democratic cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 28, 1990 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining six months of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended; a Louisiana senator from an oil-producing state, he is widely known to have been a consistent supporter of offshore drilling.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by a Democrat — Florida's two senators — but it never reached a vote, so the broader partisan divide never showed itself.

industries.note: The bill would have barred the industry from leasing, exploring, or developing a large block of federal waters off Florida and required the government to buy back existing leases. Its interest in keeping the area open runs against coastal residents and tourism businesses who bear the spill and industrialization risk.

Keeping drill rigs and the risk of spills out of the waters off Florida's southwestern beaches protects the natural asset the state's tourism economy depends on. The industry's interest and the public's interest in clean coastlines point the same way here.
An oil spill or drilling-related activity in the lease zone would threaten fisheries and reefs; the ban protected them. As with tourism, the industry gains alongside the people it serves.
